content: The house dust mite, often abbreviated as HDM by allergists, is a ubiquitous organism found in human living spaces. These mites primarily feed on organic debris, such as flakes of shed human skin, and thrive in the stable indoor environments of homes. Globally, house dust mites are recognized as the leading cause of asthma and allergic reactions. The enzymes they produce are particularly noticeable in the odor emanating from full vacuum cleaner bags. Two primary species of house dust mites are the European house dust mite (Dermatophagoides pteronyssinus) and the American house dust mite (Dermatophagoides farinae), though their distribution is not strictly limited to Europe or North America. Under a magnifying glass, a house dust mite can be observed when placed on a well-lit black background. The average size of a house dust mite is approximately 420 micrometers in length (nearly 0.5 millimeters) and 250 to 320 micrometers in width. Both male and female adult mites are globular in shape, creamy white in color, and possess a striated cuticle. As members of the class Arachnida, both larval and post-larval stages of house dust mites have eight legs. These mites can become airborne through minor air currents generated by everyday household activities. The life cycle of a male house dust mite typically spans 20 to 30 days. In contrast, a mated female can live up to 10 weeks, during which she lays 60 to 100 eggs, primarily in the last five weeks of her life. Over a 10-week lifespan, a single dust mite produces approximately 2,000 fecal particles and an even greater number of partially digested, enzyme-laden dust particles. Washing household items can effectively remove most of this waste material. However, their rapid reproduction can still have a significant impact on human health. House dust mites can survive in virtually all climates, except at high altitudes where their reproduction is inhibited. Controlling dust mites and other indoor pathogens often depends on managing relative humidity, as water availability is a critical factor for their survival. Dust mites thrive in environments where warm, moist air condenses on cooler surfaces, creating optimal conditions for their activity. When humidity levels drop below a certain threshold, dust mites slow down, become dormant, and may eventually die. They are particularly abundant in areas such as beds, kitchens, and other parts of the home where sunlight does not reach. Mites tend to remain in mattresses, carpets, furniture, and bedding, as these materials allow them to burrow deeper to avoid hazards like sunlight and vacuum cleaners. They can also move to the surface to feed on skin cells when humidity levels are high. Even in arid climates, dust mites can survive and reproduce in bedding, especially pillows, due to the moisture generated by human breathing, perspiration, and saliva during sleep. Dust mites consume microscopic particles of organic matter. Some species prefer skin cells, which are a major component of household dust, while others may feed on flour dust. Their digestive system is rudimentary, lacking a stomach, and most digestion occurs externally. To facilitate this, dust mites secrete enzymes and deposit the fungus Aspergillus repens onto dust particles. The fungus pre-digests the organic matter with its enzymes, allowing the mites to consume it. Dust mites often feed on the same particle multiple times, partially digesting it with each feeding. Between feedings, they leave the particles to decompose further. Once a particle is fully digested and no longer consumable, it is classified as fecal matter. On average, a human sheds approximately 1.5 grams of skin cells daily (equivalent to 0.3–0.45 kilograms per year), which is sufficient to sustain around one million dust mites under ideal conditions. Dust mites in bedding derive moisture from human respiration, perspiration, and saliva. House dust mites are among the most common allergens that trigger asthma. Symptoms of dust mite-related allergies include itchiness, sneezing, inflamed or infected eczema, watery eyes, a runny nose, and, in individuals with asthma, respiratory symptoms such as airway obstruction. Dust mites are also a significant contributor to hay fever.
